contentBlocks.text: Every force we've studied this week needed direct contact — a hand pushing, a foot kicking. But a magnet can move a paperclip without ever touching it. That's a very different kind of force, and today we investigate it.

A magnet pulls certain metal objects (like paperclips, some nails, and refrigerator doors) toward it without touching them — this is a force acting at a distance. If you have a magnet at home, try this: bring it slowly toward a paperclip until the clip jumps toward it before contact — notice the gap. Two magnets can also push each other away (repel) or pull together (attract), depending on which ends face each other — this is why some magnets snap together strongly one way and push apart if you flip one around. Unlike a push or a pull from your hand, magnetic force gets weaker the farther apart the objects are, and stops working past a certain distance.
Magnetism is a real force, just like a push or a pull — it just doesn't need touching to work. Tomorrow we'll review everything we've learned about forces and motion this week.

objectives: Describe magnetism as a force that acts between two objects without them touching
Explain that magnets can both attract and repel depending on orientation
materialsNeeded: A paperclip or other small metal object
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Review this week's forces so far (push/pull, balanced/unbalanced, patterns) — all needed contact.
2. Introduce magnetism as a force that does NOT need contact.
3. Demonstrate: move a magnet slowly toward a paperclip, pointing out the moment it jumps before touching.
4. If a second magnet is available, demonstrate attract vs. repel by flipping one end.
5. Discuss: does magnetism work from across the room? (No — it gets weaker with distance, and eventually stops working entirely.)
6. Complete the worksheet.
7. Close by asking the child to name where they've seen a magnet used in daily life (fridge, cabinet latch, some toys).
differentiationTips: Struggling: focus only on the attract case (paperclip jumping) before introducing repel
Ready for more: discuss that Earth itself acts like a giant magnet, which is why compasses work (a preview, not a full lesson)
If no magnets are available at home, describe the paperclip demonstration vividly and focus discussion/worksheet on the concept
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. A magnet moving a paperclip without touching it = force at a distance / non-contact force. 2. Two magnets snapping together = attract. 3. Two magnets pushing apart when flipped = repel. 4. Moving a magnet farther away makes the force weaker.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Directly addresses NGSS 3-PS2-3 and 3-PS2-4: asking questions to determine cause-and-effect relationships of electric or magnetic interactions between two objects not in contact with each other, and defining a design problem involving magnets.

generationData.instructions: Answer each question about magnets in one short sentence.

rows.problem: What do we call a magnet moving a paperclip without touching it?
What do we call it when two magnets snap together?
What do we call it when two magnets push apart?
What happens to magnetic force as you move the magnet farther away?
